replies.text: What's the difference between cement and concrete?
replies.reply: Cement is a binder—typically Portland cement, a fine powder that reacts with water. Concrete is the finished building material: a mix of cement, water, sand, and aggregate (gravel/crushed stone). Cement is roughly 10–15% of concrete by weight; the two terms are often used interchangeably in casual speech, but technically concrete contains cement rather than being it. (And since you run an architecture studio, you likely know this, Noor—happy to go deeper, e.g. into mixes or finishes.)

replies.text: How do I get red wine out of a wool rug?
replies.reply: Act fast: blot (don't rub) with a clean, dry cloth, then dilute with cold soda water while continuing to blot. Apply a small amount of wool-safe detergent or a 1:1 white vinegar mix, blotting from the outside of the stain inward. Avoid bleach, hydrogen peroxide, and heat; if a pink residue stays, a wool-safe oxy treatment sparingly can help. Always test in an inconspicuous spot, and consider a professional cleaner if the stain has set.

replies.text: Why do my ears pop on the train through a tunnel?
replies.reply: Your ears pop because trains push a piston of air ahead of them in the tunnel, causing sudden air-pressure changes. That pressure difference across your eardrum is uncomfortable until air moves through the Eustachian tube (often via swallowing or yawning) — the pop is your middle ear equalising, just like on a plane at takeoff and landing.

replies.text: Is Brutalism making a comeback?
replies.reply: Yes, quite noticeably! There's been a real revival of interest over the past decade or so — fresh appreciation for raw concrete, mass, and honesty of materials, partly driven by social media photography and nostalgia for civic ambition. You see it in retro-fits like the Barbican's cult status, new buildings borrowing Brutalist language (often softened with timber or glass), and serious preservation campaigns like SOSBrutalism. Not everyone's convinced — it still divides opinion — but among younger architects and clients it has gone from a joke to a respectable reference point. Given your own taste for the Van Nelle factory's functionalist honesty, it's probably not a huge aesthetic leap from there.

replies.text: How do passive houses stay warm?
replies.reply: Passive houses stay warm mainly through design rather than active heating. The key ingredients: super-insulation (thick walls, roofs, floors), airtight construction to stop drafts, triple-glazed windows, elimination of thermal bridges, and a mechanical ventilation system with heat recovery that recycles warmth from stale outgoing air. Orienting windows to catch winter sun also helps. The result: a small passive house typically needs almost no conventional heating — body heat, appliances, and solar gains can keep it around 20°C. The standard comes from the Passivhaus Institut in Darmstadt, which specifies a maximum heating demand of about 15 kWh/m² per year.

replies.text: Any tips for a stiff neck from drawing all day?
replies.reply: A few things that help with a stiff neck from desk/b drawing work: take a 30–60 second break every 30–45 minutes to roll your shoulders and do gentle neck side-bends (ear toward shoulder, no forceful pulling). Check your setup too — the biggest culprit is usually a screen or drawing surface set too low, so you're craning down all day. Raise your monitor or use a tilted drawing board so your gaze is closer to neutral, and keep your elbows supported. Gentle heat (a warm shower or heat pack) at the end of the day loosens the muscles better than stretching cold. If it radiates down your arm or comes with numbness, see a physio rather than pushing through.

replies.text: Explain what an acoustic rating for a wall means.
replies.reply: An acoustic rating measures how well a wall blocks sound. The most common is the Sound Transmission Class (STC) in North America, or Rw in Europe/UK — a single number in decibels, roughly how many decibels quieter sound is on the far side of the wall compared to the near side. Higher = better. Points to know as an architect: it's measured across frequency bands and weighted, so it reflects typical speech/noise; it does NOT account for low-frequency bass well (music, machinery), where combinations like Rw + Ctr are used — Ctr penalises low frequencies, relevant for timber builds. Typical values: 33–38 dB for a standard stud wall, ~50 dB for good party-wall performance, 60+ for premium sound insulation. importantly, actual performance depends on workmanship — flanking paths, sockets, and poor sealing can gut the rating. For your timber work you'll likely see Rw + Ctr quoted in specs.
